<reason>PRO (Side B) set a clean, durable frame — deductions change the price of a decision the vulnerable worker never makes, auto-enrollment changes the decision — and held it through every round. CON fought impressively: the "ceiling disguised as a floor," the net-worth/debt-offset counterfactual, taxed leakage, and stacking PRO's partial concessions were genuinely sharp and original. But CON's second rebuttal conceded the decisive point ("no deduction nudges him directly") and tried to escape by claiming both policies pass the non-participant by, conflating non-participants with workers at employers with no plan; PRO's closing caught this squarely ("everyone else has a plan, and a plan with a default") and turned CON's own inertia arguments into support for escalation lifting the stuck middle at no Treasury cost. CON's closing also mischaracterized PRO's match position as a surrender when PRO's point was consistent (match exists in both worlds, only enrollees collect it). PRO's clipped R2 is a minor execution cost, and CON never supplied a mechanism showing bigger deductions actually raise contribution rates rather than reshuffle saving. Competitive, but PRO made the vote easier.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing response to CON's "both policies pass him by" concession in [A4.1]: pointing out that "everyone else has a plan, and a plan with a default," so on CON's chosen ground (moving 4% toward 8%) escalation does the work by default while a deduction still requires an active choice — flipping CON's own inertia framing into PRO's winning position.</best_rebuttal>
